chapters.title: Chapter 3: Cointegration — Testing Whether a Pair Really Mean-Reverts

lessons.title: Case Study: Testing a Real NSE Pair for Cointegration in Python

children.text: This lesson does not introduce anything new. It runs the full pipeline built across Chapters 1 to 3, correlation, hedge ratio spread, and formal cointegration test, end to end in Python, on a fresh pair: ACC Limited and Ambuja Cements, two of India's largest cement makers, and, since Adani Group's 2022 acquisition of both from Holcim, sister companies under the same promoter group. (All price figures and statistical output in this case study are illustrative.)

body.text: A pair worth trading usually clears two different bars at once: a real economic or ownership reason the two should be linked, and a formal statistical test confirming that link shows up as genuine cointegration, not just a plausible story.

children.text: The Setup: Why ACC and Ambuja Cements

Both companies are large, NSE-listed cement manufacturers with overlapping geographic footprints, similar exposure to construction and infrastructure demand, and similar input costs, coal, petcoke, limestone, and freight. On top of that shared industry exposure, both have been under common promoter ownership since 2022, with Ambuja Cements holding a majority stake in ACC as part of Adani Group's cement consolidation, and further restructuring among the group's cement entities has been publicly discussed. That combination, shared fundamentals plus a real ownership link, is exactly the kind of structural anchor Lesson 9 described as supporting cointegration even without an extremely high correlation reading.

In practice, this comes from a broker API such as Zerodha's Kite Connect, or a data vendor, pulled as at least a year of daily closing prices for both stocks, ideally more. For this case study, assume that history is already sitting in a CSV.

body.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.read_csv("acc_ambuja_daily_closes.csv", parse_dates=["date"], index_col="date")
print(df.tail())
#              acc  ambuja
# date
# 2024-11-25  2340     520
# 2024-11-26  2355     524
# 2024-11-27  2348     519
# 2024-11-28  2362     527
# 2024-11-29  2371     531
body.caption: Loading illustrative daily closing prices for ACC and Ambuja Cements
Correlation on daily returns (Lesson 5's rule), over the full available history

body.label: Return correlation, ACC vs Ambuja Cements
body.context: Solid and credible for two large cement majors with real shared industry exposure, though correlation alone (Lesson 9) is still not proof of cointegration.

children.text: Step 3: Building the Hedge Ratio Spread

body.code:
import numpy as np

x = df["ambuja"].values
y = df["acc"].values

beta, alpha = np.polyfit(x, y, 1)
residuals = y - (alpha + beta * x)

print("beta:", round(beta, 2), "alpha:", round(alpha, 2))
# beta: 4.42  alpha: 30.1
body.caption: Fitting the hedge ratio (Lesson 6), regressing ACC's price on Ambuja's

body.label: Fitted hedge ratio (β)
body.context: For every ₹1 move in Ambuja Cements, ACC has historically moved about ₹4.42, roughly consistent with the two stocks' typical price levels (ACC trading at several times Ambuja's per-share price).

body.code:
from statsmodels.tsa.stattools import coint

score, pvalue, critical_values = coint(df["acc"], df["ambuja"])

print("Test statistic:", round(score, 2))
print("p-value:", round(pvalue, 4))
print("Critical values (1%, 5%, 10%):", critical_values)
# Test statistic: -4.62
# p-value: 0.001
# Critical values (1%, 5%, 10%): [-3.90, -3.34, -3.05]
body.caption: Running the Engle-Granger cointegration test (Lesson 11) with the correctly adjusted critical values

stats.label: Engle-Granger test statistic
stats.context: More negative than even the 1% critical value of about −3.90

stats.label: Verdict
stats.context: Reject the null of no cointegration

children.text: A passed test is not a reason to skip looking at the actual spread. Plotting the residual over the full history is a quick check for anything the p-value alone would not show, an obvious regime shift, a structural break like the ones discussed in Lesson 4, or a spread that technically clears the statistical bar but drifted meaningfully at some point along the way.

body.title: Residual spread over 24 months, ACC vs Ambuja Cements (illustrative)

body.text: This is what a genuinely healthy cointegrated spread looks like: bounded, roughly centered, with no visible drift across the full two years, not just a statistic that happens to clear a threshold.

children.text: The Verdict, and What It Does Not Mean

ACC and Ambuja Cements clear the formal test, and they have a real, ongoing structural reason to stay linked. That makes this a strong candidate to carry into Chapter 4, where sizing and running an actual pairs trade gets covered. It does not make the relationship permanent. Passing a cointegration test on historical data describes the past, not a guarantee about the future.

body.text: This particular pair carries a risk that a pair like HDFC Bank and ICICI Bank does not: corporate action risk from common ownership. Because Ambuja Cements already holds a majority stake in ACC, and further consolidation of Adani Group's cement entities has been publicly speculated, a future merger, delisting, or restructuring could remove one leg of this pair entirely, ending the trade regardless of how the spread is behaving statistically at the time. A cointegration test says nothing about this kind of risk, and it is worth checking for before treating any commonly-owned pair as a long-term candidate.

body.title: A risk the test can't see
body.scenario: The Engle-Granger test on ACC and Ambuja Cements comes back strongly cointegrated, and the residual spread chart looks clean with no drift.
body.prompt: What risk specific to this pair, that would not apply to a pair like HDFC Bank and ICICI Bank, is not captured by the statistical test at all?
body.modelAnswer: Corporate action risk from common ownership. Because both companies are controlled by the same promoter group, with Ambuja Cements already holding a majority stake in ACC, a future merger, delisting, or further restructuring could eliminate one leg of the pair entirely. HDFC Bank and ICICI Bank are independently promoted and have no comparable restructuring overhang. A cointegration test only looks at historical price behavior; it has no way of pricing in a structural corporate event that hasn't happened yet.

body.title: Reading the full pipeline
body.question: Based on this case study's results, correlation ≈ 0.78, hedge ratio β ≈ 4.42, Engle-Granger statistic ≈ -4.62 against critical values of about -3.90 (1%), -3.34 (5%), and -3.05 (10%), what is the correct conclusion?
options: The pair is correlated but there is no evidence of cointegration
The pair is both correlated and cointegrated, clearing even the strict 1% threshold
The hedge ratio is too high to be meaningful
The test is inconclusive without a rolling z-score
body.explanation: A return correlation of 0.78 is a reasonable screen, and the Engle-Granger test statistic of about -4.62 is more negative than even the 1% critical value of about -3.90, so the null of no cointegration is rejected at a high confidence level. Together with the clean-looking residual chart, this supports treating the pair as both correlated and genuinely cointegrated.

body.title: The Full Screening Pipeline
steps: Pull sufficient price history for both stocks, at least a year, ideally more
Screen with return correlation (Lesson 5) as a quick first filter
Build the regression-based hedge ratio spread (Lesson 6), not a naive price ratio
Run the Engle-Granger cointegration test with adjusted critical values (Lesson 11), not a plain ADF check
Visually sanity-check the resulting spread for drift or structural breaks
Check for corporate-action or ownership-related risks the statistics can't see before treating the pair as tradeable

points: Running the full pipeline, correlation, hedge-ratio spread, and Engle-Granger cointegration test, end to end on ACC Limited and Ambuja Cements produced a strong, consistent verdict: correlated (≈0.78) and cointegrated (test statistic ≈ -4.62, well past the 1% critical value).
A real structural anchor, here common ownership under Adani Group alongside shared industry fundamentals, strengthens the case for a pair beyond what the statistics alone show.
A passed statistical test is not a substitute for visually checking the resulting spread for drift or structural breaks over the full history.
Cointegration describes historical behavior. It does not protect against forward-looking risks like a merger or delisting, which are a genuine concern for pairs under common ownership specifically.

This closes Chapter 3's toolkit: correlation screens, the regression-based spread removes the naive ratio's flaws, and the Engle-Granger test gives a real statistical verdict, but judgment about what the numbers can't see is still required before Chapter 4's actual trade construction.
